analogy.p: Imagine a greenhouse with adjustable vents (stomata). Opening the vents lets fresh air (CO2) in, but warm moist air escapes. A hot, dry wind blowing past the vents sweeps the moist air away fast, whereas on a still, damp day the moist air just hangs around the vents and little escapes. The guard cells are the vent controllers, which swell or go limp with water. It breaks down because real guard cells open and close by osmosis, not by a person or motor, and the vents (stomata) are microscopic and numerous.
analogy.t: A leaky tap with a pressure valve

bullets: **Stomata:** small pores, mostly in the lower epidermis, that let carbon dioxide in, and oxygen and water vapour out.
**Guard cells:** a pair of cells surrounding each stoma that open and close it by changing shape.
**Four factors** that change transpiration rate: temperature, humidity, air movement (wind) and light intensity.
**Measuring:** a potometer measures water uptake, which is used as an estimate of transpiration rate.
Typical marks: 1 mark for the direction of a trend; 2 to 3 marks to explain it using diffusion gradient or stomata; 4 to 6 marks for an extended answer comparing conditions.
Link to other topics: transpiration stream (previous note), diffusion (4.1.3), photosynthesis (4.4), leaf structure (4.2.3.1), osmosis and turgor.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know (Biology only)
core.p: AQA wants you to understand the **role of stomata and guard cells in controlling gas exchange and water loss**, and to **explain the effect of changing temperature, humidity, air movement and light intensity on the rate of transpiration**. You also need data skills: reading graphs and tables, and calculating rates. This is a triple (Biology only) point, so expect application questions about unfamiliar conditions, such as a hot, windy day or a plant in a greenhouse.

bullets: Gas exchange in leaves is **by diffusion** through stomata, down concentration gradients.
Most stomata are on the **underside** of the leaf, where it is **cooler and less exposed to direct sunlight**, so less water evaporates.
The upper epidermis is covered by a **waxy cuticle**, which reduces water loss by evaporation.
Floating leaves (such as water lilies) have stomata on the upper surface because the lower surface is in water.
Stomata allow **O2 out** during photosynthesis and **CO2 out** during respiration at night.
The number of stomata per unit area is the **stomatal density**; it varies between plant species and conditions.
core.h: Stomata: where they are and what they do
core.p: A **stoma** (plural **stomata**) is a tiny pore in the leaf epidermis. Stomata let **carbon dioxide diffuse into the leaf** for photosynthesis, let **oxygen diffuse out**, and allow **water vapour to escape** (transpiration). Beneath each stoma there is an **air space** in the spongy mesophyll, which gives carbon dioxide a short route to the photosynthesising cells. Stomata are found mostly in the **lower epidermis**.

bullets: **Turgid guard cells = stoma open;** **flaccid guard cells = stoma closed.**
Water moves in or out of the guard cells by **osmosis**, not through any pump of water.
The **uneven wall thickness** (thin outer wall, thick inner wall) makes the cells bend rather than just get bigger.
Stomata are usually **open in the light**, so carbon dioxide can enter for photosynthesis.
Stomata tend to **close in the dark** (no photosynthesis, so no need for CO2) and when the plant is **short of water**, which reduces water loss and prevents wilting.
Guard cells are **kidney-shaped (bean-shaped)** when the stoma is open.
Closing stomata stops water loss, but also stops CO2 entering, so photosynthesis slows: this is the **trade-off**.
core.h: Guard cells: how they open and close the stoma
core.p: Each stoma is surrounded by two **guard cells**. These are the only epidermal cells with **chloroplasts**, and they change shape as they gain or lose water. When water **enters the guard cells by osmosis** they become **turgid** and swell. The cell wall on the inner side (next to the pore) is **thicker** and less stretchy than the outer wall, so as the cells swell they **bow outwards** and the pore opens. When the guard cells lose water they become **flaccid**, straighten and the pore closes.

bullets: Open stomata: more CO2 in (faster photosynthesis), but more water vapour out (more transpiration).
Closed stomata: very little water loss, but photosynthesis eventually stops because CO2 cannot get in.
A wilting plant has lost more water than it takes in; its cells have become **flaccid**.
Wilting can be a useful short-term response because it reduces the exposed leaf area.
Plants cannot avoid water loss completely because the **mesophyll cells must stay moist** for gas exchange (gases dissolve before diffusing into cells).
Farmers and gardeners water crops and use greenhouses to control the factors affecting transpiration.
core.h: The leaf's balancing act: gas exchange versus water loss
core.p: A leaf has a problem: it needs a large, thin, permeable surface for **gas exchange**, but a moist, permeable surface also loses **water**. Plants cope by controlling the size of the stomatal pores. When water is plentiful and light is bright, open stomata favour photosynthesis. When water is scarce, closed stomata save water but reduce photosynthesis and growth. This is why plants in drought grow slowly.

bullets: **Temperature:** higher temperature gives molecules more kinetic energy, so **faster evaporation and diffusion**.
**Light intensity:** brighter light makes the stomata **open wider** (and increases photosynthesis), so more vapour escapes.
**Air movement (wind):** wind blows away the humid air near the leaf, **keeping the concentration gradient steep**.
**Humidity:** more water vapour in the air makes the gradient **shallower**, so transpiration decreases.
Transpiration rate is the **volume of water lost per unit time** (for example cm³ per hour).
Remember the pattern: factors that increase the **diffusion gradient** or **evaporation** increase transpiration.
core.h: Factors affecting the rate of transpiration: overview
core.p: Transpiration happens in two stages: **evaporation** of water from the mesophyll cells and **diffusion** of water vapour out through the stomata. Anything that speeds up evaporation or makes the diffusion gradient steeper, or opens the stomata wider, increases the rate. The four factors you need to know all work in one of these ways. In an exam, always say **which stage** the factor affects.

bullets: Temperature up gives more kinetic energy, so **faster evaporation** and faster diffusion, so **rate increases**.
Light up gives **stomata open wider**, so more diffusion of water vapour, so **rate increases**.
In the **dark** stomata close so transpiration falls to a low level (a little water still escapes through the cuticle).
A graph of rate against light intensity often **levels off** because the stomata are fully open or another factor limits the rate.
Warm, bright, sunny days give the **highest transpiration**; cool, dark days give the lowest.
Photosynthesis also increases with light, using up some water, but this is tiny compared with the water lost.
core.p: As **temperature rises**, water molecules gain **kinetic energy** and move faster, so water **evaporates more quickly** from the mesophyll cells and the vapour **diffuses out faster**. Warm air can also hold more water vapour, so the gradient between the leaf and the air stays steeper. **Light intensity** affects transpiration indirectly: in bright light the guard cells become turgid and **open the stomata wider**, so more water vapour can diffuse out. In the dark most stomata close, so transpiration is very low.

bullets: Humidity up gives a **shallower concentration gradient**, so **slower diffusion** and **lower transpiration**.
Dry air gives a steeper gradient, so faster transpiration.
Wind (air movement) up gives it **removes water vapour** from near the leaf, so gradient stays steep, so rate increases.
In still, humid conditions a **humid layer** surrounds the leaf and transpiration is slowest.
On a hot, dry, windy day plants can lose water faster than the roots can supply it, so they **wilt**.
Always write 'diffusion gradient' or 'concentration gradient' when explaining humidity and wind.
core.p: **Humidity** is the amount of water vapour in the air. Inside the leaf the air spaces are almost saturated with water vapour. If the outside air is dry, the **concentration gradient is steep** and water vapour diffuses out quickly. If the outside air is humid, the gradient is **shallow**, so diffusion is slower. **Air movement** blows away the humid air that collects around the stomata and replaces it with drier air, so the **diffusion gradient is kept steep** and transpiration speeds up. In still air a layer of humid air builds up next to the leaf and slows the rate.

bullets: **Describe first:** 'as light intensity increases from 1 to 4 units, the rate increases from 2 to 8 mm³ per minute'.
**Then explain:** 'because the stomata open wider so more water vapour diffuses out'.
If a line levels off, say 'the rate stops increasing' and give a reason (stomata fully open, or another factor such as water supply or temperature is limiting).
**Percentage change** = (new − old) ÷ old × 100.
**Rate from a graph:** use the gradient of a tangent (change in y ÷ change in x) with units.
Identify the **independent variable** (the factor changed), the **dependent variable** (rate of transpiration) and **control variables**.
Be careful with units: mm³ per minute, cm³ per hour, g per hour.
core.p: Exam questions give you a table or graph of transpiration rate against one factor and ask you to describe and explain the pattern. Start with a clear description using numbers, then give the biological reason. Read scales carefully, and when a graph levels off, say so and suggest a limiting factor. You may also be asked to calculate a rate of change or a percentage change.

bullets: **Cut the shoot underwater at a slant**: stops air entering the xylem (air would break the water column) and gives a larger surface area for uptake.
**Assemble the potometer underwater** so the apparatus is full of water with no air bubbles.
**Keep the leaves dry** and make joints **airtight with vaseline**, so uptake is only due to transpiration and nothing leaks.
Introduce **one air bubble** by lifting the capillary end out of the water for a moment, then put it back.
**Record the bubble's start position**, time it for a fixed period (for example 5 minutes) and record the distance moved.
Use the **reservoir tap** to reset the bubble to the start between repeats; repeat three times and calculate a **mean**.
Volume of water taken up = **π × r² × distance** (r is the radius of the capillary tube), so rate = volume ÷ time.
core.p: A **potometer** measures the **rate of water uptake** by a cut shoot. It is used as an **estimate** of the rate of transpiration because almost all the water a plant takes up is lost by transpiration (a tiny amount is used for photosynthesis and to keep cells turgid). As the shoot takes up water, an **air bubble** in a thin capillary tube moves along a scale. The distance moved in a set time gives the rate of uptake.

bullets: **Light intensity:** move a lamp to different measured distances from the plant (closer means brighter); use a heat shield or water bath to keep temperature constant.
**Air movement:** use a fan (or hairdryer on cool setting) at different distances or speeds; compare with still air.
**Humidity:** enclose the leaves in a clear plastic bag (humid air) compared with open air; or spray the leaves.
**Temperature:** carry out the experiment in rooms or enclosures at different temperatures, recording temperature with a thermometer.
Control: same shoot, same leaf area, same time period, the other three factors constant.
**Safety:** keep water away from electrical equipment; take care when cutting the shoot with a scalpel.
Repeat readings and ignore anomalies when calculating a mean.
core.h: Investigating each factor with a potometer
core.p: To investigate one factor you change it (independent variable) while keeping the others constant (control variables), and measure the rate of water uptake (dependent variable). You should allow the shoot a few minutes to settle after changing a condition. Because plants differ, the same shoot should be used where possible, or shoots of similar size and leaf area.

bullets: It measures **water uptake**, not water loss: some water is used for photosynthesis or stored in cells.
A **cut shoot has no roots**, so it may not behave like a whole plant.
**Leaks or air bubbles** in the apparatus cause errors.
The shoot may **close its stomata** if cut or stressed, lowering uptake.
The bubble can **stick** in the capillary or be hard to read to the nearest mm.
Other conditions (for example room temperature) may change during the experiment.
Alternative method: **mass loss** of a potted plant or leaf over time (rate = change in mass ÷ time).
core.p: A good evaluation answer says what the potometer does not show perfectly. Because it is an indirect method, you need to give reasons why the results are only an **estimate** of transpiration. These evaluation points are common 2-mark questions.

bullets: Area of field of view = **π × r²** (using radius, or π × (diameter ÷ 2)²).
Stomatal density = **number of stomata ÷ area of the field of view**.
Use the same magnification and take **several fields of view** to find a mean.
Compare lower and upper epidermis: lower usually has far more stomata.
Plants in hot, dry habitats often have fewer stomata or stomata in sunken pits, which reduces water loss (apply to unfamiliar plants).
Link to magnification calculations: image size = magnification × actual size.
core.p: You may be asked to count stomata to compare species or leaf surfaces. A thin layer of clear nail varnish painted on the leaf, peeled off when dry and viewed under a microscope shows the pattern of stomata. You count the stomata in the field of view and divide by the area of the field of view to get the number per mm². This helps to show why the lower epidermis has more stomata than the upper.

bullets: Hot: more kinetic energy, so faster evaporation and diffusion.
Dry air (low humidity): steeper concentration gradient, so faster diffusion.
Windy: removes the water vapour, keeping the gradient steep.
Sunny: stomata open wider, so more vapour escapes.
Result: very high transpiration, so water may be lost faster than the roots absorb it, so cells become flaccid and the plant **wilts**.
Response: guard cells lose water and become flaccid, so stomata close to save water, but then photosynthesis falls because CO2 cannot enter.
core.h: Linking it all together: a hot, windy day
core.p: A common 6 mark question asks what happens to a plant on a hot, dry, windy, sunny day. Build the answer step by step: each factor increases the rate by a different mechanism, and the plant has a way to respond. Writing the factors in a clear list and giving a reason for each secures marks.

exam: Command words: **Describe** (say what the graph or table shows with numbers), **Explain** (give the biological reason using 'because'), **Evaluate** (strengths and weaknesses of the method), **Calculate** (show working and units).
1 mark: direction of a trend (increases/decreases). 2 marks: trend plus reason. 3 to 4 marks: reason using concentration gradient AND stomata/evaporation.
For humidity and wind always use the words **concentration gradient** (or diffusion gradient), **water vapour** and **diffuse**.
For guard cells write: 'water enters by **osmosis**, cells become **turgid**, they change shape and the stoma **opens**'.
Say 'guard cells' not 'stomata open on their own', and use 'turgid' and 'flaccid' correctly.
For the potometer, name three precautions: **cut underwater**, **keep leaves dry**, **airtight seals**, and only one bubble.
Potometer calculation: volume = π × r² × distance; rate = volume ÷ time. Keep units consistent (mm, mm³, min).
Evaluation questions: mention **uptake is not the same as loss**, a cut shoot has no roots, and the apparatus may leak.
For a 6 mark question, structure it: factor, effect on evaporation/diffusion/stomata, effect on rate, then consequence for the plant (wilting, stomata closing).
Graph tip: quote data from the graph (with units) and say whether the trend levels off; suggest a limiting factor if it does.
Identify variables: independent (factor changed), dependent (rate of uptake) and control (the other three factors, same shoot, same time).

mistakes.r: Guard cells are turgid when the stoma is open, and flaccid when it is closed.
mistakes.w: Guard cells are open when they are flaccid.

mistakes.r: Higher humidity gives a shallower concentration gradient so less diffusion of water vapour and a lower rate of transpiration.
mistakes.w: Higher humidity increases transpiration because there is more water.

mistakes.r: Wind removes the water vapour near the stomata, keeping the concentration gradient steep, so the rate increases.
mistakes.w: Wind makes the water evaporate because it is cold.

mistakes.r: A potometer measures water uptake, which is used as an estimate of transpiration rate.
Stomata are mostly on the lower epidermis, where it is cooler and less water evaporates.
mistakes.w: Stomata are mostly on the upper surface.

mistakes.r: More light makes the guard cells turgid so the stomata open wider, allowing more water vapour out (heat also speeds evaporation).
mistakes.w: More light makes transpiration faster because the plant gets hot.

mistakes.r: Water enters through the roots; stomata allow carbon dioxide in and oxygen and water vapour out.
mistakes.w: Stomata let the plant take in water.

mistakes.r: The leaves must be dry; wet leaves block the stomata and change the rate of evaporation.
mistakes.w: Use a wet leaf in the potometer experiment.

summary: AQA Biology only: you must explain how stomata and guard cells control gas exchange and water loss, and how temperature, light intensity, humidity and air movement change the rate of transpiration (including using a potometer and interpreting data). It matters because it shows the trade-off every plant faces between taking in carbon dioxide for photosynthesis and losing water.

terms.d: A small pore in the leaf epidermis, surrounded by two guard cells, through which gases and water vapour diffuse.
One of a pair of cells surrounding a stoma that changes shape to open or close it.
Describes a cell that is full of water and pushes against its cell wall; turgid guard cells open the stoma.
Describes a cell that has lost water and is limp; flaccid guard cells close the stoma.
The loss of water vapour from the leaves of a plant, mainly through the stomata.
The volume (or mass) of water lost by a plant per unit time.
The amount of water vapour in the air.
The difference in concentration between two regions; particles diffuse from high to low concentration.
Apparatus that measures the rate of water uptake of a cut shoot by the movement of an air bubble along a scale.
The waxy layer on the leaf surface that reduces water loss by evaporation.
Drooping of a plant when cells lose water and become flaccid.
The layer of cells on the underside of the leaf, containing most of the stomata.
The photosynthesising tissue of the leaf, made up of palisade and spongy layers.
The energy of movement; particles with more kinetic energy move faster.
The number of stomata per unit area of leaf surface.
The variable that is deliberately changed in an investigation.

worked.ans: 4.7 mm³ per minute (4.71 to 3 significant figures)
worked.q: A potometer has a capillary tube of radius 0.5 mm. The air bubble moves 36 mm in 6 minutes. Calculate the rate of water uptake in mm³ per minute. (3 marks)

worked.ans: On a hot, dry, windy day evaporation is faster because of the higher temperature, and the concentration gradient of water vapour between the air spaces in the leaf and the outside air is steeper because the air is dry and the wind removes the water vapour. Water vapour therefore diffuses out through the stomata faster, so the rate of transpiration is higher.
worked.q: Explain why a plant loses water faster on a hot, dry, windy day than on a cool, humid, still day. (4 marks)
steps: Hot: water molecules have more kinetic energy, so evaporation from the mesophyll and diffusion of water vapour are faster (1).
Dry air: low humidity gives a steeper concentration gradient of water vapour between the leaf air spaces and the air (1).
Windy: air movement removes water vapour from near the stomata so the concentration gradient is kept steep (1).
So water vapour diffuses out through the stomata faster, giving a higher rate of transpiration (1).

worked.q: A student views an impression of a leaf. The field of view has a diameter of 0.50 mm and contains 14 stomata. Calculate the number of stomata per mm². (3 marks)
